analysis.one_liner: Narrows social media platforms' legal immunity so harassment, discrimination, and scam victims can sue.
analysis.headline: The SAFE TECH Act, which would have let victims of online harassment, discrimination, and wrongful death sue social media platforms, drew just 2 cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have scaled back Section 230, the law that shields social media platforms from lawsuits over content their users post. It would have let victims sue platforms over stalking, harassment, discrimination, wrongful death, and scams carried through paid or promoted content, and would have forced platforms — not plaintiffs — to prove the immunity applies in court. It never received so much as a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People targeted by online stalking, harassment, or intimidation; people discriminated against through platforms' ad-targeting or housing and job listings; consumers defrauded through paid posts and ads; families bringing wrongful-death claims tied to platform-facilitated harm; and competitors using antitrust law. All would gain a path to sue platforms that current law largely cuts off [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of online harassment and discrimination

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes platform immunity for claims of stalking, cyberstalking, harassment, intimidation, discrimination, antitrust violations, and wrongful death, giving victims a way to hold platforms accountable in court.
It strips immunity from paid or promoted content — posts a platform accepts payment to make available or helped create — so people harmed by scam ads or discriminatory ad targeting could sue.

It forces a platform to raise Section 230 as an affirmative defense and carry the burden of proving it applies, instead of letting courts dismiss victims' cases at the start, and it lets courts order platforms to remove material likely to cause irreparable harm.

analysis.who_pays: Social media companies and other internet platforms would bear the cost: more lawsuits, injunctions requiring content removal, and the legal expense of proving the defense in each case. Those costs would partly reach smaller sites and forums too, and platforms might respond by removing more lawful speech to avoid being sued [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and internet platforms

drawbacks.text: The carve-out for 'paid' content is broad: most of the internet is monetized in some way, so the change could expose a huge range of websites — not just the biggest platforms — to lawsuits over ordinary user content.

Making the platform prove the defense in every case, and opening the door to injunctions against hosting material, raises litigation costs and could push platforms to over-remove lawful speech, which falls hardest on small sites and on speakers who rely on online forums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a group the current law leaves with no remedy: harassment and stalking victims, people targeted by discriminatory ads, and families in wrongful-death cases. The costs are real too — the paid-speech carve-out is written broadly enough to sweep in much ordinary online content, and the added litigation burden would fall on small platforms as well as large ones. A narrower bill could have delivered most of the victim protections with less risk of chilling lawful speech, but as written the tradeoff is genuine rather than one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its communications subcommittee the day after introduction, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald McEachin introduced the SAFE TECH Act on May 20, 2021, joined by Reps. Kathy Castor and Mike Levin as cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, the next day, to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends with that subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media platforms came out ahead: they kept the broad Section 230 immunity the bill would have trimmed, while victims of online harassment, discrimination, and platform-facilitated harm remained unable to sue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media platforms keeping broad legal immunity

for.name: Rep. A. Donald McEachin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to scale back Section 230 immunity for platforms.

for.name: Reps. Kathy Castor and Mike Levin

for.name: Civil rights and online-safety advocacy organizations
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed Section 230 reform to give harassment and discrimination victims a path to court.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to sit in the communications subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Internet platform companies and tech trade associations
against.role: Major social media and internet companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed changes to Section 230 that would expose them to lawsuits over user content and paid ads.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all three sponsors were House Democrats and the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors, so its true level of support was never tested.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and online services
industries.note: The bill would strip these companies' broad immunity from lawsuits over user content in cases involving harassment, discrimination, wrongful death, and paid speech. Their interest in preserving that immunity runs directly against the interests of victims seeking a day in court.

Content a platform is paid to carry or helps create — targeted ads, promoted posts — would lose immunity, exposing ad-targeting practices like discriminatory delivery to litigation. The ad business is how the largest platforms make their money, so this hits their core revenue model's legal footing.

industries.industry: Small websites, forums, and hosting services
industries.note: The bill carves them no special protection: they could face the same lawsuits and defense burdens as large platforms, without big companies' legal budgets. Some might also benefit if the antitrust carve-out lets them sue dominant platforms.
